overview: Megalosaurus bucklandii was the first dinosaur formally described to science — named by William Buckland in 1824 from a partial lower jaw and postcranial elements found in the Stonesfield Slate of Oxfordshire. It was a large Mid-Jurassic theropod, about six metres long, living at the margin of the warm Tethys Sea roughly 166 million years ago.

For over a century "Megalosaurus" was a wastebasket taxon into which virtually every European theropod fragment was placed. Systematic revision in the late 20th century restricted the genus to Stonesfield Slate material, leaving it as a tetanuran of uncertain family-level placement.

fossilSites.name: Stonesfield Slate (Taynton Limestone Formation)
fossilSites.note: Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) quarry deposits with the type jaw and postcranial material; original holotype still displayed at the Oxford University Museum of Natural History.

fossilSites.name: Great Oolite Group
fossilSites.note: Bathonian limestone series preserving fragmentary Megalosaurus remains across central England.

articles.title: The first named dinosaur
articles.body: Buckland presented his description at the Geological Society of London in February 1824. The word "dinosaur" did not yet exist — Owen coined it in 1842, using Megalosaurus as one of the three founding members. Charles Dickens referenced it walking down Holborn Hill in the opening of Bleak House (1852), reflecting its hold on Victorian imagination.

articles.title: Known anatomy
articles.body: Material includes a partial dentary with large recurved serrated teeth, vertebrae, an ilium and limb elements. The teeth are laterally compressed, blade-like and strongly recurved — classic large theropod morphology. No complete skull is known, so most life reconstructions are inferred from relatives.

articles.title: Palaeoenvironment
articles.body: The Stonesfield Slate was deposited in warm, shallow-marine to coastal settings on the margin of the Tethys Sea. Megalosaurus was likely the apex terrestrial predator of this coastal ecosystem, sharing its world with the sauropod Cetiosaurus, fish, marine reptiles and abundant invertebrates.

fossilRecord.formations: Taynton Limestone Formation/Stonesfield Slate, Oxfordshire, England
fossilRecord.material: Fragmentary jaw, teeth and postcranial bones.
fossilRecord.paleo: Middle Jurassic European terrestrial to nearshore environments.
fossilRecord.evidence: Large theropod jaw and limb bones made it one of the first dinosaurs scientifically described.

record.mya: middle Bathonian, about 168-166 million years ago
record.description: Megalosaurus bucklandii was a large megalosaurid from the Taynton Limestone Formation of Oxfordshire. Modern revision restricts the genus to the type dentary and a limited set of comparable local bones, not the worldwide wastebasket once called Megalosaurus.
facts: The lectotype is a partial right dentary with teeth.
Some cranial, vertebral, pelvic and limb bones from the same regional unit are referred, but no complete skeleton exists.
Most historical species named Megalosaurus have been removed or are dubious.

review.ageReviewNote: The reviewed age follows the middle Bathonian Taynton Limestone and does not import unrelated Megalosaurus referrals.

residualUncertainty: Association of referred bones with the dentary-bearing taxon is not direct.
Maximum adult size is not constrained by a complete individual.

evidence.material: Lectotype dentary plus limited referred cranial and postcranial bones from the same regional unit.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not use the old global wastebasket record or call it a complete skeleton.
evidence.summary: Megalosaurus bucklandii was a large megalosaurid from the Taynton Limestone Formation of Oxfordshire. Modern revision restricts the genus to the type dentary and a limited set of comparable local bones, not the worldwide wastebasket once called Megalosaurus.
